questions.q: What distinguishes reinforcement learning from supervised learning?
options: RL requires more data than supervised learning
RL has no labeled correct answers; the agent learns from a reward signal instead
RL only works on image data
RL does not involve a model being trained
questions.explain: Supervised learning trains on labeled (input, correct output) pairs. RL has no such labels — the agent learns by trying actions and observing a reward signal.

questions.q: In the agent-environment loop, what does the environment return after the agent takes an action?
options: The correct action it should have taken
A new state and a reward
A gradient update
A labeled training example
questions.explain: After an action, the environment transitions to a new state and emits a reward. There is no 'correct action' feedback in RL.

questions.q: What is the credit assignment problem?
options: Deciding how much GPU budget to allocate to training
Determining which past actions deserve credit for a reward received later
Assigning labels to unlabeled training data
Splitting a dataset into train and test sets
questions.explain: Because reward is often delayed, the agent must figure out which earlier actions in a sequence actually contributed to a later reward — this is the credit assignment problem.

questions.q: In RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) applied to an LLM, what plays the role of the 'reward'?
options: The number of tokens generated
A human preference judgment about the quality of a response
The model's training loss
The size of the training dataset
questions.explain: In RLHF, the reward signal comes from human preference judgments over model outputs, which stand in for the environment's reward in the standard RL loop.

questions.q: Which of the following problems is best framed as reinforcement learning rather than supervised learning?
options: Predicting a house's sale price from its labeled features
Classifying emails as spam or not spam using labeled examples
Teaching a robot to walk through trial and error, with no labeled 'correct' joint angles
Clustering customers into segments based on purchase history
questions.explain: A robot learning to walk through trial and error, guided only by feedback on how well it's doing, has no labeled correct answers — it's a sequential decision problem suited to RL.
